title: Subsidiarity (CCC 1883–1885)
hook: decisions should be made at the lowest level that can handle them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the common good: the conditions that let everyone flourish. Your line was everyone flourishing. What did you leave a little better than you found it? Today closes the week. Day one thousand one hundred twenty.

Moses is sitting from morning until evening, and the line of people waiting for him never ends. Every quarrel, every dispute, comes to him. His father-in-law, Jethro, watches for a day and says, more or less: this isn't good. You'll wear yourself out, and these people with you. So Jethro gives him a plan, in the book of Exodus. Choose able, honest people, set them over groups large and small, and let them settle the ordinary matters. Only the hard cases come up to you. Moses listens, and does it. The Catechism doesn't tell this story, but it names a principle that sits comfortably beside it. A long word for a simple idea.
screen: `MORNING UNTIL EVENING.` → `THIS ISN'T GOOD.` → `THE HARD CASES COME UP.`

segments.voice: The word is subsidiarity. The Catechism sets it inside a worry. Societies need to work together, but too much intervention by the state, it says, can threaten personal freedom and initiative. So the Church's teaching has worked out a principle. A community of a higher order shouldn't interfere in the internal life of a community of a lower order, taking over its functions. Instead, it should support that smaller community when it needs help, and help coordinate its work with the rest of society, always with a view to the common good. In plain words: the family does what a family can do. The neighborhood, the parish, the town, what they can do. The larger body steps in to help, not to swallow. Then the Catechism holds up a model for it, and the model isn't a theory of economics. It's how God governs. God, it says, has not willed to reserve to himself all exercise of power. He entrusts to every creature the functions it is capable of performing, according to its own nature. God's way of governing, it says, shows great regard for human freedom, and it should inspire the wisdom of those who govern communities. Last, it marks the edges. Subsidiarity is opposed to all forms of collectivism, it says, and it sets limits for the state's intervention. It also isn't an excuse for the bigger body to walk away; support in time of need is part of the definition. Yesterday's common good says what society is for. Today's subsidiarity says who should do it first: the closest hands that can.
screen: `TOO MUCH CONTROL THREATENS FREEDOM.` · `THE LARGER HELPS, IT DOESN'T SWALLOW.` · `GOD SHARES HIS POWER.` · `LIMITS ON THE STATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let someone decide for themselves. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where you tend to take over. A child's homework. A coworker's slide deck. A partner's way of loading the dishwasher. A friend's plan you'd do differently. Ask: can they handle this? If the answer is yes, picture yourself stepping back. Hands off. Available if they ask. Notice how that feels: maybe relief, maybe itchy fingers. If you pray, you can ask for the patience to let others do what they can. The bell holds the time.
Subsidiarity. A higher community shouldn't take over what a smaller one can do, but should help it when it needs help. The Catechism roots it in the way God shares his power. Today's word.

Your line: closest hands first. This week moved through feelings, conscience, virtue, the Spirit's gifts and fruits, mercy and sin, the common good, and now subsidiarity. Today, let one person do one thing their own way. Day one thousand one hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Subsidiarity is a principle of Catholic social teaching; Catholics invoke it in debates about the roles of families, local communities, charities and governments.

fork.reveal: in Exodus 18, Moses takes Jethro's advice: able, honest people judge the ordinary matters, and the hard cases come to Moses.

trapdoor: what you thought: a bureaucratic word for local control.
what it means: what smaller communities can do, they should do, with the larger ones helping, not taking over.
what a scholar hears: CCC 1883 drawing on Catholic social teaching, God sharing his power in 1884, and the limits on state intervention in 1885.

notes: CCC 1883–1885 paraphrased (copyrighted translation): danger of excessive state intervention and the principle stated (1883, from Centesimus Annus 48), God not reserving all power, great regard for freedom (1884), opposed to collectivism, limits to state intervention (1885). Confirm.
